title: Java is pass-by-value, including object references
answer: Java is always pass-by-value. For primitive arguments, the method receives a copy of the primitive value. For object arguments, the method receives a copy of the reference value, not the caller's variable itself. Because both reference copies can point to the same object, the method can mutate that object's state. However, reassigning the method parameter to a new object changes only the local copy of the reference and does not reassign the caller's variable. Java therefore does not have C++-style pass-by-reference parameter semantics.
